content: The Trent Accreditation Scheme (TAS) is a non-profit organization based in the United Kingdom. Its primary mission is to uphold and continuously improve quality standards in healthcare delivery. This is achieved through the surveying and accreditation of healthcare organizations, particularly hospitals, both within the UK and internationally. Trent's mission is similar to that of the USA's Joint Commission International (JCI) and other major international healthcare accreditation bodies. However, there are notable differences in its approach. In addition to UK hospitals, Trent also surveys a significant number of private sector hospitals in Hong Kong. The approach taken by Trent towards hospital accreditation is grounded in the belief that no single healthcare system—whether European, American, Asian, or otherwise—has the exclusive right to define acceptable quality and best clinical practices. Similarly, no one country has the authority to dictate how hospitals in another country should operate. What is essential is that the quality of care provided to patients meets the highest possible standards. Furthermore, hospitals must independently determine how to maintain these standards and address new challenges as they arise. If a hospital's overall standards are shown to be of acceptable quality, it is both desirable and ideal that local differences, such as those related to culture and legislation, are explicitly considered and incorporated into the assessment standards in an appropriate manner. To achieve this, Trent collaborates closely with participating hospitals to develop a mutually acceptable set of standards for evaluation. These standards are regularly reviewed and updated in collaboration with representatives from partner hospitals, reflecting the ever-changing nature of healthcare. Trent has developed various methods to ensure local participation and even ownership of the accreditation process in each locality. The organization employs surveyors from the UK who are either currently working in the British National Health Service (NHS) or have recently retired, bringing valuable frontline experience. In Hong Kong, Trent also appoints locally-based surveyors who are actively working in local hospitals. These surveyors are trained and always survey hospitals other than their own, fostering the exchange of ideas and best practices among hospitals in the same region and promoting camaraderie. Trent surveyors are all volunteer professionals rather than salaried employees. Their surveys go beyond simply working through a checklist of standards. Instead, they involve direct, face-to-face conversations with staff at all levels, including clinical medical staff and senior management. Qualified medical doctors are included in all survey teams to ensure a comprehensive evaluation. Surveyors are granted full access to the hospital under review and are free to speak with anyone they choose. This approach emphasizes critical thinking and avoids a rigid, checklist-driven culture. The data generated during the survey is analyzed and discussed not only by the Trent team but also by the hospital being surveyed. This collaborative process reflects Trent's philosophy that accreditation is about improving patient services and enhancing the organization's ability to work effectively towards that goal. Trent surveyors evaluate a wide range of hospital activities and governance, including management, facilities, equipment, audits, research, education, training, and clinical/medical activities. In Hong Kong, survey teams typically consist of two or three UK-based surveyors working alongside two locally-based surveyors. One surveyor is designated as the lead. At the end of the survey, the lead surveyor presents the key findings to the hospital, usually on the final day. This oral presentation allows hospitals to begin implementing remedial actions immediately. The findings are later compiled into a detailed printed report, highlighting both strengths and areas for improvement. After a round of surveys, a joint meeting is held where the printed reports of all surveyed hospitals are discussed in depth by the Trent Board, which includes both local and UK representatives, along with senior representatives from the surveyed hospitals. A decision is then made on whether accreditation will be granted unconditionally or subject to conditions. Trent's approach ensures that local hospitals have a sense of ownership over the accreditation process. This contrasts with schemes that impose standards, surveyors, and decisions unilaterally from outside. By fostering local involvement, Trent helps build the confidence of participating hospitals in their ability to maintain and improve quality. This collaborative approach also ensures that Trent surveyors are consistently present in all participating hospitals. Trent is a member of the United Kingdom Accreditation Forum (UKAF). With the rise of medical tourism, international healthcare accreditation has become increasingly important. Several organizations fulfill this role globally, including the Canadian Council on Health Services Accreditation (CCHSA), the Joint Commission International (JCI) in the USA, the Australian Council on Healthcare Standards (ACHS), and the Trent Accreditation Scheme (TAS) in the UK. Additionally, the Society for International Healthcare Accreditation (SOFIHA) provides a platform for discussion and the sharing of ideas and best practices among providers and users of international healthcare accreditation.
